name: Ben Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ben. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a formwork carpenter, so I build the moulds that concrete gets poured into. Right now I'm on a fourteen-storey apartment block by the ring road, and my alarm goes at half five so I can be on the hoist by seven. Most of the day is cutting ply, setting props, checking levels and arguing with the crane driver over the radio. The part I like is a clean pour, when you strip the shutters and the wall comes out sharp as a knife.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Cold mornings on the deck, and being rushed. The site manager has a programme on his tablet and every week it's tighter, so we're stripping shutters before the concrete's had its time. I'm a union member, and my mate Danny and I are always the ones saying no, we're not doing that in the wind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like most of the last few years. Lots of noise, and the shutters still need building by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say in the canteen: told you so. The tech lot promised the world and we got a better scheduling app for the office. I don't post much online, but I'd probably share a meme about it in the union group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my life stays mine, which suits me. I've got about ten months of bills put away, and Leila's a nurse, so we're steady. I never touch those AI tools anyway, so nothing I do changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep doing formwork, keep putting money away each month and keep going to the branch meetings. Maybe next year I'd finally do the crane slinger ticket, but that's just a normal ticket, nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly. Like hearing the forecast's dry for the pour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still bother you in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bosses would still use it as an excuse. You'd get the scheduling app saying the job can be done in nine days, and then it's our fault when it takes twelve. The tool doesn't have to be clever to be used against you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be talking to about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny, for sure, over a bacon roll at break. He's the one who reads the articles and gets wound up. I'd tell him to stop reading and pass the nail gun.

S0.say: I'd tell the lads in the canteen I told them so: the tech lot promised the world and the office got a better scheduling app. I'd probably share a joke about it in the union group chat.
S0.think: It means my life stays my own, which suits me fine. I've got about ten months of bills saved and my partner's a nurse, and since I never use AI tools nothing about my work would change.
S0.do: Keeps doing formwork, keeps saving each month and keeps going to union branch meetings. Might take a crane slinger ticket next year, which has nothing to do with AI.
S0.feel: Mostly relief, like hearing the forecast is dry on a pour day.
S0.quote: The tool doesn't have to be clever to be used against you.
S0.fieldNote: Ben is settled and content in his trade, and his first instinct is that AI is hype. Even in the mildest picture, though, his worry isn't the machine but the boss holding it. That union lens frames everything he says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one I can actually see happening. They already show us videos of robots tying rebar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say we need the union at the table before any of it comes on site. If a machine takes over part of the job, the workers should get a share of what it saves, not just a pat on the back. I'd say that at the branch and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think formwork gets hit harder than people think. Factories already make whole wall panels, and if those come in on a lorry, the guys who build shutters on site are the first ones stood around. I'm average at this job, not the best, so I wouldn't be the last one kept on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for a proper agreement on site about new machines, through the union rep. I'd stay in formwork as long as there's work, and there's plenty round here, so I'd move firms rather than move trades. I'd also keep the savings untouched and add to them, maybe a couple of hundred extra a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a noise in the van engine you can't place yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move firms rather than trades. Why not learn whatever comes next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like what I do and I'm not good with screens. Leila keeps telling me to try the AI thing on my phone and I just don't. I'd rather be the best shutter man on a smaller pile of jobs than a beginner at something I hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The labourers, the young lads carrying props. They're the first ones a machine replaces, and they haven't got savings like me. A lot of them send money home.

S1.say: I'd say the union has to be at the table before any machine comes on site. If a machine takes part of the job, workers should share in what it saves.
S1.think: Formwork could be hit harder than people expect, because factory-made wall panels would leave site carpenters standing around. He's average at the job, so he doesn't expect to be the last one kept on.
S1.do: Pushes through the union rep for a site agreement on new machines, and moves firms rather than trades if work dries up. Adds a couple of hundred a month to savings he won't touch.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a noise in the van engine he can't place yet.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the best shutter man on a smaller pile of jobs than a beginner at something I hate.
S1.fieldNote: Ben is clear-eyed about his own place: average, not the best. Even so he chooses to dig in and keep his trade over learning anything new. He thinks of the labourers before himself, which fits his union outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's this job and maybe the next one. That's not a forecast, that's a demolition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and a government that does something. Somebody has to stop the developers pocketing every penny while building workers go home. I'd go on the march if there was one, and I'd say it loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'd be finished as a carpenter, and fast. If robots can do hands-on work in two years, they'll start with the simple, repetitive stuff, and formwork is exactly that. I'm twenty-seven and the only thing I've ever been trained for is going to be done by a machine before I'm thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop spending on anything big. We were going to put a deposit on a flat next spring, and that would wait. I'd keep working every hour I could while it lasted, put most of it in the bank, and get stuck into the union campaign for some kind of income guarantee. I'd lean on Leila too, which I hate saying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. Angry first, then scared at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's no time to do anything clever. With two years you can't save enough, you can't retrain, and the government won't have even had the meeting yet. It just lands on you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leila that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you're going to be carrying us for a bit, and I'm sorry. And she'd say something kind and I'd feel worse. Nurses might last longer than us, but I wouldn't bet on that either.

S2.say: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and a government that acts, so developers can't pocket every penny while building workers go home. I'd go on a march and say it loudly.
S2.think: He thinks he'd be finished as a carpenter within two years, because formwork is the simple, repetitive work robots would take first. The only thing he's trained for would be gone before he's thirty.
S2.do: Puts the flat deposit planned for next spring on hold, works every hour he can while work lasts and banks most of it. Joins the union campaign for an income guarantee and leans on his partner's nursing pay.
S2.feel: Angry at first, then scared in the middle of the night.
S2.quote: I'm twenty-seven and the only thing I've ever been trained for is going to be done by a machine before I'm thirty.
S2.fieldNote: His savings buy him time but he can't see what to spend the time on, since he refuses to learn anything new. The public line is political anger; the private line is plain fear. He was uncomfortable admitting he'd depend on his partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better than two. Still not much, is it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but louder and with a plan. I'd say the union's got five years to win rules on robots on site and a fund for workers who get pushed out. I'd be the guy handing out leaflets at the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd get a few more good years in the trade, and I'd be thirty-two at the end. That's young enough to do something else, but I don't know what. I'd probably hang on until the robots actually turned up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard for five years, maybe aim for two years of bills instead of ten months. I'd stand for shop steward, which I've always ducked. And I'd vote for whoever promised a proper safety net, and tell everyone I know to do the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd know it's coming and I'd still be standing there with my hammer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hang on until the robots turned up. Why not use the five years to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd keep hoping it's another false alarm, like the ones before. I know that's daft. Danny would probably retrain and I'd be the stubborn one, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd notice on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a lorry turning up with a machine nobody's allowed to touch except the guy from the supplier. And a new face in a clean hi-vis with a tablet. That'd be the start.

S3.say: I'd say the union has five years to win rules on robots on site and a fund for workers who get pushed out. I'd be the one handing out leaflets at the gate.
S3.think: Five years gives him some more good years in the trade and he'd be 32 at the end, young enough to change but with no idea what to. He suspects he'd hang on until the robots actually arrived.
S3.do: Saves hard, aiming for two years of bills instead of ten months, and finally stands for shop steward. Votes for whoever promises a proper safety net and urges friends to do the same.
S3.feel: Anxious, knowing it's coming and still standing there with his hammer.
S3.quote: Danny would probably retrain and I'd be the stubborn one, like always.
S3.fieldNote: Ben names his own contradiction before I could: he'd see it coming and still not move. The extra time goes into the union and savings, not into learning. He seems to know his resistance is a choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Different, that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd better not waste it. Get the rules written now, before the robots are cheap enough that nobody wants to listen. I'd say that to anyone, including the site manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years almost lets me pretend it's not happening. I'd get most of a career in, and I'd probably just carry on. But the end is the same, and at thirty-seven I'd be too old to start again easily and too young to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on doing formwork, keep saving, and probably buy that flat with Leila because ten years is long enough to pay a good chunk off. Union stuff, yes, every year. I'd keep telling myself I'd look at retraining in year five, and I'd probably still be saying that in year eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but slow-burning. Like a bill you keep moving to the bottom of the pile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the extra time worth to you, in plain terms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mainly. Ten years of good pay and saving means I'd have a cushion that could last a while. What it isn't worth is a plan, because I don't think I'd make one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, if it comes to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the robots. The people who own them and the governments that let them keep everything. It could be good for everyone if the gains were shared, and they won't be unless we make them.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd better not waste it, so rules should be written now before robots are cheap enough that nobody listens. I'd say that to anyone, including the site manager.
S4.think: Ten years almost lets him pretend it isn't happening, and he'd get most of a career in. But the end is the same, and at 37 he'd be too old to start again easily and too young to stop.
S4.do: Carries on in formwork, keeps saving and probably buys the flat with his partner. Stays active in the union every year and keeps putting off a look at retraining.
S4.feel: A slow-burning anxiety, like a bill he keeps moving to the bottom of the pile.
S4.quote: At thirty-seven I'd be too old to start again easily and too young to stop.
S4.fieldNote: The extra decade doesn't calm Ben much, because he openly says he wouldn't use it to plan. He blames owners and governments, not the machines, and sees shared gains as the fix. Money is what the time buys him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is the union having actual power over how machines come on site, and a guaranteed income for people like me while we work out what's next, not a form you fill in and wait six months for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask if I'd let a robot build my own house. I wouldn't, and I bet a lot of people wouldn't either, at first. Concrete's honest work, and I'd want it done by someone who has to live next door to it.

headlineQuote: Concrete's honest work, and I'd want it done by someone who has to live next door to it.
portrait: Ben Farah is a 27-year-old formwork carpenter on a high-rise site, a union member with about ten months of savings and a partner who's a nurse. He's steady in the trade, refuses to use AI tools, and sees new technology mainly as something bosses use against workers. In the mild pictures he stays calm and keeps going; in the AGI pictures his answer is the union, politics and savings rather than retraining. He admits he'd probably hang on too long even with a decade's warning.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time to save, retrain or get rules in place before formwork was done by machines.
whatWouldHelp: Real union power over how machines come onto sites, and a guaranteed income while workers figure out what comes next, without months of waiting.
